canonical_statement: The study aimed to document the extent and pattern of unfractionated-heparin underprescribing in obese inpatients with venous thromboembolism at an academic teaching hospital.
The investigators used a three-year cross-sectional consecutive case series based on hospital records.

Eligible patients were adult inpatients with BMI >=30 kg/m2 treated at Winthrop University Hospital with unfractionated heparin for pulmonary embolism or deep vein thrombosis from January 1, 2004 through December 31, 2006.

outcome.definition: PTT >60 seconds; in the hospital laboratory this corresponded to factor Xa >0.3 units

canonical_statement: Time to therapeutic anticoagulation was defined as the interval from heparin initiation to the first PTT >60 seconds.

Medical records were reviewed using a standardized form to capture demographics, diagnostic method, heparin start time, initial bolus and infusion, first PTT >60 seconds, and the final infusion sustaining PTT 60-90 seconds.
For bolus assessment, actual prescribed doses were compared with a recommended dose of 80 units/kg of body weight.

canonical_statement: The investigators used nonparametric correlations and simple linear regression to examine relationships among weight, initial and final infusion doses, and time to therapeutic anticoagulation.
A log transformation of time-to-therapeutic-anticoagulation was used for regression because the time interval data were skewed.
The study included 84 obese patients with documented VTE who received unfractionated heparin.

canonical_statement: The prescribing pattern was interpreted as physicians often choosing initial doses close to the eventual therapeutic dose rather than intentionally overshooting the target to achieve therapeutic anticoagulation rapidly.
In an informal convenience interview of 8 of 81 internal medicine residents, all 8 reported awareness of weight-based guidance but said bleeding concerns led them to reduce doses in obese patients.
The study was conducted at a single academic teaching hospital, so the authors could not be certain that local resident prescribing practices were representative elsewhere.
The study included only patients with BMI >=30 kg/m2 and did not determine whether prescribing patterns differed in non-obese patients.
Post-discharge follow-up was not systematically collected, so recurrent VTE incidence was not measured as a study outcome.
Major bleeding was not tracked as a study objective; the authors noted that the study was not designed to assess the relationship between dose and bleeding risk.
The authors emphasized that the study compared actual treatment with recommended treatment and was not designed to validate or dispute the dosing guideline itself.

The authors concluded that many obese patients had delays beyond 24 hours in reaching adequate anticoagulation and that most received an initial bolus or infusion below contemporaneous weight-based recommendations.
